claim: Zebrafish larvae with prior experience of live prey consume considerably more prey than naive larvae.
source: We report that larvae with prior experience of live prey consume considerably more prey than naive larvae.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Increased prey consumption in experienced larvae is mainly due to increased capture success and a modest increase in hunt rate.
source: This is mainly due to increased capture success and a modest increase in hunt rate.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: The initial turn to prey and the final capture manoeuvre of the hunting sequence were jointly modified by experience.
source: We demonstrate that the initial turn to prey and the final capture manoeuvre of the hunting sequence were jointly modified by experience and that modification of these components predicted capture success.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Modification of the initial turn to prey and final capture manoeuvre predicted capture success.
source: We demonstrate that the initial turn to prey and the final capture manoeuvre of the hunting sequence were jointly modified by experience and that modification of these components predicted capture success.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: Early experience plays an instrumental role in permanently embedding specific information about the environment in the developing animal.
source: The study of animal ethology has demonstrated an instrumental role of early experience in permanently embedding specific information about the environment in the developing animal, and in extending and enhancing behavioral repertoires (Purves, 1985; Bateson, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Predation behavior benefits from learning by experience across diverse species.
source: An example of a dynamic behavior that is found to benefit from learning by experience is predation as, across diverse species, it involves predicting and responding to the behavior of another animal.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the introduction.

claim: In altricial species, young animals learn to hunt from direct experience and from mimicking the behavior of parents or other conspecifics.
source: In altricial species, which require an extended period of parental care, young animals learn to hunt from direct experience, and from mimicking the behavior of parents or other conspecifics (Danchin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Hatching snakes improve their ability to capture prey with experience.
source: For example, with experience, hatching snakes improve in their ability to capture prey (Mehta, 2009) and orb-web spiders build more effective webs (Heiling and Herberstein, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Orb-web spiders build more effective webs with experience.
source: For example, with experience, hatching snakes improve in their ability to capture prey (Mehta, 2009) and orb-web spiders build more effective webs (Heiling and Herberstein, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Lack of prior exposure to prey before release into the wild can strongly reduce survival chances of hatchery-raised fish to adulthood.
source: Studies of hatchery-raised fish have found that a lack of prior exposure to prey, before being released into the wild, can strongly reduce their chances of surviving to adulthood (see Coughlin, 1991; Brown et al., 2003; Blaxter, 1986; Meyer, 1986; Dutton, 1992; Cox and Pankhurst, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In some fish species, detection, handling and capturing of prey is enhanced only for the particular type of prey they have experienced.
source: It is unlikely that exposure to prey simply facilitates certain aspects of behavioral ontogeny that would have developed with time (Bateson, 1981), because in at least some fish species, the detection, handling and capturing of prey is enhanced only for the particular type of prey they have experienced (Meyer, 1986; Cox and Pankhurst, 2000; Drost, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ontogeny of hunting behavior relies on relevant early experience to fully develop.
source: Such evidence suggests that the ontogeny of hunting behavior relies on relevant early experience to fully develop (Brown et al., 2003; Warburton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Larval zebrafish is an ideal vertebrate model for the detailed study of behavior and its associated circuits.
source: The larval zebrafish is an ideal vertebrate model for the detailed study of behavior and its associated circuits.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for using zebrafish in the study.

claim: Larval zebrafish have a diverse behavioral repertoire that can be precisely measured.
source: They have a diverse behavioral repertoire that can be precisely measured (Orger and de Polavieja, 2017; Marques et al., 2018), and neural activity can be recorded non-invasively and at single-neuron resolution throughout the whole brain (Ahrens et al., 2013; Wolf et al., 2015; Portugues et al., 2014; Naumann et al., 2016; Kawashima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neural activity in larval zebrafish can be recorded non-invasively and at single-neuron resolution throughout the whole brain.
source: They have a diverse behavioral repertoire that can be precisely measured (Orger and de Polavieja, 2017; Marques et al., 2018), and neural activity can be recorded non-invasively and at single-neuron resolution throughout the whole brain (Ahrens et al., 2013; Wolf et al., 2015; Portugues et al., 2014; Naumann et al., 2016; Kawashima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Larval hunting appears as a distinct behavioral mode composed of several component actions chained together into a sequence.
source: Larval hunting appears as a distinct behavioral mode that is composed of several component actions chained together into a sequence (Borla et al., 2002; McElligott and O'malley, 2005; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Significant progress has been made in characterizing the kinematics of larval zebrafish hunting in detail.
source: While significant progress has been made in characterizing the kinematics of larval zebrafish hunting in detail (Bianco et al., 2011; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013; Patterson et al., 2013; Borla et al., 2002; Mearns et al., 2020), and in describing the circuits and cell types involved in this behavior (Bianco and Engert, 2015; Antinucci et al., 2019; Romano et al., 2015; Semmelhack et al., 2014; Preuss et al., 2014; Muto et al., 2017; Muto et al., 2013; Henriques et al., 2019), it is not known whether experience affects the ontogeny (Westphal and O'Malley, 2013) and effectiveness of their hunting sequences.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It is not known whether experience affects the ontogeny and effectiveness of zebrafish larval hunting sequences.
source: While significant progress has been made in characterizing the kinematics of larval zebrafish hunting in detail (Bianco et al., 2011; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013; Patterson et al., 2013; Borla et al., 2002; Mearns et al., 2020), and in describing the circuits and cell types involved in this behavior (Bianco and Engert, 2015; Antinucci et al., 2019; Romano et al., 2015; Semmelhack et al., 2014; Preuss et al., 2014; Muto et al., 2017; Muto et al., 2013; Henriques et al., 2019), it is not known whether experience affects the ontogeny (Westphal and O'Malley, 2013) and effectiveness of their hunting sequences.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Hunting episodes begin with a convergent saccade and a turn, which accounts for a large proportion of the orienting response toward prey.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we find that hunting episodes begin with a convergent saccade and a turn, which accounts for a large proportion of the orienting response toward prey.
evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with previous reports.

claim: The convergent saccade is maintained throughout the hunting sequence during which larvae home in on the target using a series of temporally discrete swim bouts.
source: The convergent saccade is maintained throughout the hunting sequence during which larvae home in on the target using a series of temporally discrete swim bouts, which successively minimize the distance to prey, up to a point where they can perform a final capture manoeuvre.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Experience resulted in a modest increase in the probability of initiating hunting behavior.
source: We found that experience resulted in a modest increase in the probability of initiating hunting behavior, suggesting that the ability to detect prey or the motivation to hunt may be influenced by prior experience.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The main effect of experience was a marked increase in the probability of a hunt sequence resulting in successful capture.
source: However, the main effect of experience was a marked increase in the probability of a hunt sequence resulting in successful capture.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: Experienced larvae make an initial turn-to-prey that undershoots prey azimuth.
source: Firstly, at the onset of hunting we found that they make an initial turn-to-prey that undershoots prey azimuth.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Inexperienced larvae display initial turns that do not undershoot, but rather align them more with prey azimuth.
source: Paradoxically, inexperienced larvae display initial turns that do not undershoot, but rather align them more with prey azimuth.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Experienced larvae are more likely to employ high-speed capture swims that also tend to be initiated at a longer distance from prey.
source: Secondly, we find that experienced larvae are more likely to employ high-speed capture swims that also tend to be initiated at a longer distance from prey.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: In experienced larvae capture speed is coordinated with distance to prey.
source: We show that in experienced larvae capture speed is coordinated with distance to prey, and is also combined with undershooting in their turn-to-prey behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Coordinated behaviors of capture speed, distance to prey, and undershooting contribute to the capture success of hunt-sequences.
source: We then identify that these coordinated behaviors contribute to the capture success of hunt-sequences, and can be used to predict larval hunting efficiency.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Zebrafish larvae were reared in three different feeding regimes: live-fed (LF), not-fed (NF), and dry-fed (DF).
source: Zebrafish larvae were reared in one of three different feeding regimes: a live-fed (LF) group, which received Rotifers, a group that was not-fed (NF), and a third group that received dry growth food (DF).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: No decrease in survival rates of larvae in the NF group was observed.
source: Consistent with previous observations we did not observe a decrease in survival rates of larvae in the NF group (Hernandez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an observation consistent with previous work.

claim: A small, but statistically significant, effect on growth was determined by comparing means of standard lengths at 7dpf between groups.
source: However a small, but statistically significant, effect on growth was determined by comparing means of standard lengths (SL) (Parichy et al., 2009) at 7dpf between groups (NF = 4.15 mm, LF = 4.37 mm, DF = 4.21 mm see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: In all groups the evoked hunt-rate is markedly increased compared to the spontaneous hunt rate.
source: We find that in all groups the evoked hunt-rate is markedly increased compared to the spontaneous hunt rate.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The success rate for the LF group was 32%, with 21% for the NF group, and 18% for the DF.
source: As shown on Figure 3A, the success rate for the LF group was the highest at 32%, with 21% for the NF group, and 18% for the DF.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The estimated probability of a successful hunting event is clearly increased in the LF group compared to the NF and DF groups.
source: Figure 3B shows that the estimated probability of a successful hunting event is clearly increased in the LF group compared to the NF and DF groups.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Larvae from the LF group have a mean consumption rate that is almost double that of the NF and DF groups.
source: Consumption estimates reveal that larvae from the LF group have a mean consumption rate that is almost double that of the NF and DF groups.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In all three groups the majority of successful hunting episodes involve fast capture swims.
source: Figure 4A–C reveal that in all three groups the majority of successful hunting episodes involve fast capture swims and that the majority of failed hunting episodes involve slow capture swims.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The LF group has the largest proportion of high-speed captures (approximately 41%).
source: Although slow capture types form the majority of capture swims in all groups, the LF group, which has highest percentage of capture success, also has the largest proportion of high-speed captures (LF≈41% , DF≈21% and NF≈28% ), and the highest ratio of fast captures over slow captures in successful episodes (approximately ×5 LF, ×1.69 DF and ×3 NF).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: A correlation between prey-distance and capture-speed exists overall and it is stronger in the LF group.
source: Figure 4H confirms that a correlation between these variables exists overall and it is stronger in the LF group.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Time to reach prey does not vary with distance travelled during the capture swim, and this is more clearly demonstrated in the LF group's fast capture swims.
source: Figure 4I suggests that time to reach prey does not vary with distance travelled during the capture swim, and this is more clearly demonstrated in the LF group's fast capture swims.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 4I.

claim: A large turn that re-orients a larvae toward prey commonly occurs at the beginning of the hunting sequence.
source: A large turn that re-orients a larvae toward prey commonly occurs at the beginning of the hunting sequence (Bianco et al., 2011; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013; Patterson et al., 2013) (see Figure 5A; Appendix 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with previous reports and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The initial turn is proportional to prey azimuth.
source: This initial turn is proportional to prey azimuth (Patterson et al., 2013; Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The initial turns recorded in the LF group are distinct in undershooting prey azimuth.
source: The distributions of likely turn-ratios estimated by the model shown on Figure 5E confirm that the initial turns recorded in the LF group are distinct in undershooting prey azimuth; the slope of the regression model gives a mean 0.73 for LF, 0.87 NF, and 0.92 for DF.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Hunt events from the NF and DF groups display initial turns that do not consistently undershoot, but rather align larvae closer to the prey's azimuth.
source: Paradoxically, hunt events from the NF and DF groups display initial turns that do not consistently undershoot, but rather align larvae closer to the prey's azimuth.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Undershooting on the first turn to prey is a kinematic adaptation of the hunting sequence that develops from rearing with live prey.
source: These findings suggest that undershooting on the first turn to prey is a kinematic adaptation of the hunting sequence that develops from rearing with live prey.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The relationship between undershooting and fast-capture swim is not innate but rather driven by experience.
source: This relationship is not innate but rather driven by experience because although DF and NF larvae may occasionally undershoot on their first-turn to prey, this turn is not systematically associated with a fast-capture swim.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Experience drives the development of correlations between undershooting and fast-capture swims.
source: Thus, experience drives the development of correlations between undershooting and fast-capture swims, which suggests that experience is not confined to modifying components of the hunt sequence independently but is also able to combine them.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The LF group has higher overall capture speed and distance, and lower turn ratio compared to control groups.
source: Figure 7A shows a 3D rendering of the resulting posterior parameter distributions per group, according to which the LF group (green) has higher overall capture speed and distance, and lower turn ratio (see Figure 7—figure supplement 1 for a more detailed view of parameter space).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Larvae from the LF group are more efficient hunters, they undershoot on their first turn to prey and execute fast capture swims from a relatively longer distance to prey.
source: Members of the LF group are shown to be more efficient hunters, they undershoot on their first turn to prey (black), and execute fast capture swims (yellow) from a relatively longer distance to prey (cyan), thus suggesting a relationship of these behaviors with hunting efficiency (red).
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Two principal components of a larva's mean behavior can be used to predict its capture efficiency.
source: Linear regression model shows that two principal components of a larva's mean behavior, as in B, can be used to predict its capture efficiency.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: This is the first time experience has been shown to affect hunting ability at 7 dpf in zebrafish.
source: This can be observed as early as 7 dpf, and to our knowledge, it is the first time experience has been shown to affect hunting ability at that early developmental stage.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: Differences in consumption are mostly due to experience-dependent changes in hunting skill.
source: By utilizing statistical inference to characterize the effects of rearing diet on the hunt-effort and capture success of each group, we were are able to provide the first comprehensive evidence that differences in consumption are mostly due to experience-depended changes in hunting skill (see Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Zebrafish larvae raised with Paramecia performed prey capture behaviors more frequently than those that had not.
source: This finding is consistent with previous observations that zebrafish larvae raised with Paramecia performed prey capture behaviors more frequently than those that had not (Patterson et al., 2013), and suggest that prior experience may condition prey response, which would be in agreement with findings in other fish species (see Winfield and Townsend, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Starved larvae are more likely to shift behavioral decisions from avoidance to approach.
source: However, our finding that hunt rates are not elevated in the NF group is seemingly at odds with studies showing that starved larvae are more likely to shift behavioral decisions from avoidance to approach (Filosa et al., 2016) and increase their food intake compared to fed larvae (Jordi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Within 40 min differences in the bout patterns expressed between starved and fed larvae become undetectable.
source: This apparent discrepancy can be reconciled by the fact that we allow all feeding groups to acclimatize with live prey for 1-2hr prior to recording in the evoked conditions. This time period has been shown to be sufficient to overcome motivational differences between starved and fed larva, as within 40 min differences in the bout patterns expressed between these groups become undetectable (Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: An intrinsic timer process, similar to the stochastic-state switching mechanism, is likely controlling hunt-episode duration.
source: We suggest that an intrinsic timer process, similar to the stochastic-state switching mechanism recently proposed to underlie the switching of foraging state between exploration and exploitation (Marques et al., 2020), is likely controlling hunt-episode duration, and allows for these to be modulated by factors such as prey stimuli, satiety (Johnson et al., 2020) and experience.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: The superior capture efficiency of LF against the NF group is not explained by differences in growth.
source: The superior capture efficiency of LF against the NF group is not explained by differences in growth, because larvae in the nutrition control group (DF), which tend to be larger than larvae in the NF group (see Appendix 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), have the lowest capture efficiency of the three groups.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The most likely explanation for superior capture efficiency is that it is caused by changes to the hunting routine.
source: Therefore, the most likely explanation is that superior capture efficiency is caused by changes to the hunting routine.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Utilizing a fast capture speed may be important for some evasive prey species.
source: For some evasive prey species utilizing a fast capture speed may be important (Drost, 1987; Westphal and O'Malley, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Atlantic salmon, carp and pike larvae improve their capture success by using fast capture-speeds.
source: There is already evidence that Atlantic salmon, carp (Cyprinus earpio) and pike (Esox IUC US) larvae improve their capture success by using fast capture-speeds (Coughlin, 1991; Drost, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rotifers are not known to exercise any effective evasive response to imminent predator capture strikes.
source: However, in this study we used Rotifers, which, unlike other prey types (Drenner et al., 1978; Drost, 1987), they are not known to exercise any effective evasive response to imminent predator capture strikes (Coughlin, 1994; Lapesa et al., 2002; Yúfera et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Adult Rotifers can move at 0.5–1.5 mm/sec depending on their size among other factors.
source: Adult Rotifers, can move at 0.5–1.5 mm/sec (≈1.5–2 body lengths), depending on their size among other factors (Yúfera et al., 2005; Lapesa et al., 2002), which is in agreement with our measured estimates of mean prey speeds (see Appendix 5).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and data from the study.

claim: An increase in capture distance can lead to improvements in capture success rates because it effectively diminishes errors in aiming caused by prey motion.
source: Therefore, an increase in capture distance can lead to improvements in capture success rates because it effectively diminishes errors in aiming caused by prey motion, especially against faster moving prey.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Larva zebrafish adjust their swim-speed as a function of prey distance in order to coordinate the time of reaching prey against their max-gape timing.
source: Since the gape-cycle timing is reportedly stereotyped (Hernández, 2000), we therefore suggest that larva zebrafish adjust their swim-speed as a function of prey distance in order to coordinate the time of reaching prey against their max-gape timing.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: Undershooting behavior is an off-axis approach strategy that enhances capture success by actively improving the perception of prey distance.
source: We hypothesize that this undershooting behavior is an off-axis approach strategy that enhances capture success by actively improving the perception of prey distance.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis.

claim: Prey proximity predicts prey choice when hunting is initiated in the presence of multiple targets.
source: Prey proximity predicts prey choice when hunting is initiated in the presence of multiple targets (Bolton et al., 2019), while the length and intervals of the swim bouts executed during prey approach progressively shorten with prey-distance (Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013; Bolton et al., 2019; Johnson et al., 2020), eventually leading to stopping at a distance appropriate for a capture strike, the success of which, as we discussed in the previous section, also appears to dependent on prey-distance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Image size is an important feature for triggering hunting in zebrafish larvae.
source: Although image size is an important feature for triggering hunting in zebrafish larvae (Bianco et al., 2011; Romano et al., 2015), distance perception through image size may not be sufficient, because vision in zebrafish is monocular with a fixed focus and so retinal image size is an ambiguous cue for the true size of an object.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Vision in zebrafish is monocular with a fixed focus.
source: Although image size is an important feature for triggering hunting in zebrafish larvae (Bianco et al., 2011; Romano et al., 2015), distance perception through image size may not be sufficient, because vision in zebrafish is monocular with a fixed focus and so retinal image size is an ambiguous cue for the true size of an object.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Prey velocity cues obtained passively during inter-bout intervals are likely used for distance perception.
source: Although prey velocity cues obtained passively during inter-bout intervals are likely used (Trivedi and Bollmann, 2013), these would provide ambiguous distance estimates because prey-speed can vary significantly even among prey of the same species (see Appendix 5—figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Larval bouts are not ballistic but utilize visual feedback during motion.
source: This prey approach strategy predicts that bout-motion and distance perception operate in real-time closed-loop (Ahissar and Assa, 2016) and is consistent with evidence that larval bouts are not ballistic but utilize visual feedback during motion (Portugues and Engert, 2011; Portugues et al., 2015; Jouary et al., 2016), and with evidence that loss of visual feedback during approach can impair larvae from reaching capture distance (Jouary et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Loss of visual feedback during approach can impair larvae from reaching capture distance.
source: This prey approach strategy predicts that bout-motion and distance perception operate in real-time closed-loop (Ahissar and Assa, 2016) and is consistent with evidence that larval bouts are not ballistic but utilize visual feedback during motion (Portugues and Engert, 2011; Portugues et al., 2015; Jouary et al., 2016), and with evidence that loss of visual feedback during approach can impair larvae from reaching capture distance (Jouary et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The retina could be directly computing the speed of moving edges.
source: The retina could be directly computing the speed of moving edges (Portugues et al., 2015), while tuned specifically to prey-like stimuli by integrating retinal image motion with image size, which is in agreement with evidence that specific combinations of stimulus size and speed are required for hunting initiation (Bianco and Engert, 2015; Barker and Baier, 2015; Semmelhack et al., 2014; Antinucci et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Specific combinations of stimulus size and speed are required for hunting initiation.
source: The retina could be directly computing the speed of moving edges (Portugues et al., 2015), while tuned specifically to prey-like stimuli by integrating retinal image motion with image size, which is in agreement with evidence that specific combinations of stimulus size and speed are required for hunting initiation (Bianco and Engert, 2015; Barker and Baier, 2015; Semmelhack et al., 2014; Antinucci et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Learning does not seem to modify individual behavioral components of the hunting sequence independently.
source: In either case, the evidence here suggest that learning does not seem to modify individual behavioral components of the hunting sequence independently.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The relationship between undershooting and fast long-range capture swims is not intrinsic.
source: This correlation is in not intrinsic, long-range capture swims are not an inevitable consequence of undershooting, because the opposite correlation (overshoot with fast-capture swims) also exists and is most often seen in prey-naive animals (NF,DF).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Hunting strategies that combine fast capture swims executed from a longer distance are more likely to lead to consumption of prey.
source: We find that hunting strategies that combine fast capture swims executed from a longer distance are more likely to lead to consumption of prey (Figure 7B, Figure 4), and thus their ontogeny could be based on positive reinforcement through operant conditioning (Skinner, 1938).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Previous attempts to establish classical or operant learning in larval zebrafish by pairing visual cues to electric shock failed to show learning at this early stage.
source: However, previous attempts to establish classical or operant learning in larval zebrafish, by pairing visual cues to electric shock, failed to show learning at this early stage (Valente et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A classical conditioning study showed enhanced tail response to the conditioned stimulus after pairing a tactile stimulus on the side of the body with a visual cue of a moving spot.
source: A different, classical conditioning study showed enhanced tail response to the conditioned stimulus after pairing a tactile stimulus on the side of the body with a visual cue of a moving spot (Aizenberg and Schuman, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Learning is constrained to expecting specific information about the environment to instruct the parameters of particular behavior of the developing animal.
source: Thus, although in theory a form of arbitrary behavioral chaining could be used to generate efficient behavior in a wide variety of experienced conditions (Enquist et al., 2016), it would appear here that learning is constrained to expecting specific information about the environment to instruct the parameters of particular behavior of the developing animal (Bateson, 1981; Todd and Gigerenzer, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings supported by citations.

claim: Early foraging experience could allow larvae to learn and adapt their behavior to the food sources available in their environment.
source: In this case, early foraging experience could allow larvae to learn and adapt their behavior to the food sources available in their environment.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The effect of a brief (two days) hunting experience is to rescue, or trigger the maturation of, initially ineffective hunting behavior.
source: Although natural variability in learning speed is expected, our analysis on individual larvae suggests that the effect of a brief (two days) hunting experience is to rescue, or trigger the maturation of, initially ineffective hunting behavior.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Pretecto-hindbrain and pretecto-hypothalamic pathways have been associated with the release of hunting behavior in response to visual prey stimulation.
source: Localizing the neural circuits that support experience-dependent changes to evoked hunt-rates (Figure 2E) draws attention towards the pretecto-hindbrain and the pretecto-hypothalamic pathways. This is because both of these have been associated with the release of hunting behavior in response to visual prey stimulation (Muto et al., 2017; Semmelhack et al., 2014; Antinucci et al., 2019; Filosa et al., 2016), and thus changes in their activity could be underlying the modulation of hunt-rates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A companion study did not find differences in tectal and pre-tectal activity between experienced and naive larvae during hunt-initiation.
source: Yet, a companion study, which imaged the brains of partially restrained larvae (7 dpf) during hunt-initiation, did not find differences in tectal and pre-tectal activity between experienced and naive larvae (Oldfield et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a companion study.

claim: The functional connectivity between optic tectum and pre-tectum appears to increase in experienced larvae.
source: Nevertheless, consistent with the higher evoked hunt-rates of experienced larvae, the functional connectivity between optic tectum and pre-tectum appears to increase, along with the probability that pretectal activation is followed by eye-vergence (Oldfield et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a companion study.

claim: Forebrain activity in experienced larvae was higher during eye-vergence (hunting) compared to naive larvae.
source: The main difference observed was that forebrain activity (telencephalon and the habenula) in experienced larvae was higher during eye-vergence (hunting) compared to naive larvae.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a companion study.

claim: Ablation of the forebrain in experienced larvae demonstrated that although forebrain recruitment is not necessary for initiating hunting, it does contribute to the frequency of these events.
source: Further, ablation of the forebrain, in experienced larvae, demonstrated that although forebrain recruitment is not necessary for initiating hunting, it does contribute to the frequency of these events (Oldfield et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a companion study.

claim: Experience-dependent adaptations to the hunt-rate are manifested via a tectal pathway that goes through the forebrain.
source: Combined with evidence of increased functional connectivity between tectal periventricular neurons (PVN) and the forebrain's telencephalon in experienced larvae (Oldfield et al., 2020), it appears that experience-dependent adaptations to the hunt-rate are manifested via a tectal pathway that goes through the forebrain.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation supported by a citation to a companion study.

claim: Pathways may be functionally classified into those supporting innate behavior and others supporting learned adaptations to it.
source: This pathway appears to operate in parallel to those supporting innate hunt initiation, reflecting an organizational principle according to which pathways may be functionally classified into those supporting innate behavior and others supporting learned adaptations to it.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Diencephalic dopaminergic neuron recruitment could only explain changes in general swimming activity, and not finer locomotor behavior during prey approach.
source: In terms of their effect on locomotion, evidence from ablation experiments suggest that diencephalic dopaminergic neuron recruitment could only explain changes in general swimming activity, and not finer locomotor behavior during prey approach (Jay et al., 2015), while detailed studies using tactile and visual stimuli suggest that dopaminergic action on swimming behavior maybe indirect, through sensory and proprioceptive processes (Reinig et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The serotonergic system has been shown to be involved in modulating the release of hunting in response to visual prey recognition in a manner that depended on a larva's feeding-state.
source: Perhaps a better candidate would be a forebrain pathway that targets the serotonergic system, which has been shown to be involved in modulating the release of hunting in response to visual prey recognition in a manner that depended on a larva's feeding-state (Filosa et al., 2016) or its internal foraging state (Marques et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Visual-evoked orienting turns towards prey have been attributed to the tectal-hindbrain pathway.
source: Visual-evoked orienting turns towards prey have attributed to the tectal-hindbrain pathway, which forms a sensory-map with a functionally segregated anatomy, of distinct descending retinotopically organized projections for approach and avoidance behavior, that can signal graded visual-evoked orienting turns towards prey (Helmbrecht et al., 2018; Orger, 2016; Fajardo et al., 2013; Orger et al., 2008; Romano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The development of the tectal sensory-map is generally not driven by visual experience.
source: However, the development of this sensory-map is generally not driven by visual experience (see Marachlian et al., 2018; Pietri et al., 2017), and, in agreement with this, the tectal activity maps for prey location are not altered by experience (Oldfield et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The tectal activity maps for prey location are not altered by experience.
source: However, the development of this sensory-map is generally not driven by visual experience (see Marachlian et al., 2018; Pietri et al., 2017), and, in agreement with this, the tectal activity maps for prey location are not altered by experience (Oldfield et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a companion study.

claim: Changes in the tectal encoding of prey position do not underlie the differences in turn-behavior between prey-naive and experienced larvae.
source: Given this evidence, changes in the tectal encoding of prey position do not underlie the differences in turn-behavior between prey-naive and experienced larvae observed in this study.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The modulation of turn-gain is most likely manifested downstream, perhaps at the level of reticulospinal neurons via the modulatory action of a pathway that runs parallel to the primary tectal-hindbrain one.
source: We posit that the modulation of turn-gain is most likely manifested downstream, perhaps at the level of reticulospinal neurons via the modulatory action of a pathway that runs parallel to the primary tectal-hindbrain one, such as the aforementioned diencephalic dopaminergic neurons (Reinig et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis.

claim: Activation of hypothalamic dopaminergic neurons has been associated with capture success.
source: Fortunately, the zebrafish community has already achieved such feats (Cong et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017), with the first data of brain activity indicating a few seconds of sustained activity in hypothalamus, midbrain, and hindbrain following prey capture (Cong et al., 2017), while more recently, activation of hypothalamic dopaminergic neurons has been associated with capture success (Marques et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Similar sustained hypothalamic dopaminergic activity has been previously observed in partially restrained animals following vigorous motor activity.
source: However, imaging during unconstrained behavior is no panacea, because making causal inferences could become harder in comparison to more constrained experimental designs, which provide more control. For example, similar sustained hypothalamic dopaminergic activity has been previously observed in partially restrained animals following vigorous motor activity (Reinig et al., 2017), so fast-capture manoeuvres may be sufficient to explain some of the brain activity observed during unconstrained prey capture.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Prior experience of live prey modifies and associates components of the larval zebrafish hunting sequence in manner that improves their capture success.
source: In summary, we have demonstrated that prior experience of live prey modifies and associates components of the larval zebrafish hunting sequence in manner that improves their capture success.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the main findings.

claim: The ontogeny of hunting behavior relies on learning by experience to fully develop.
source: Our findings suggest that the ontogeny of hunting behavior relies on learning by experience to fully develop.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: Learning may be constrained to particular tasks at the early stage of 7 dpf.
source: Combined with prior attempts that failed to show conditioning in larval zebrafish (Valente et al., 2012), it appears that learning may be constrained to particular tasks at this early stage, but nevertheless it is sophisticated enough to alter a multidimensional behavioral parameter space so that innate goal-oriented behavior is improved.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Interactions between an innate behavior and learning are very common to the ontogeny of behavior.
source: Such interactions between an innate behavior and learning are very common to the ontogeny of behavior (Hinde, 1973) and it is likely that the general learning principles, which allow experience to shape brain development, are conserved across species (Warburton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: General learning principles that allow experience to shape brain development are likely conserved across species.
source: Such interactions between an innate behavior and learning are very common to the ontogeny of behavior (Hinde, 1973) and it is likely that the general learning principles, which allow experience to shape brain development, are conserved across species (Warburton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.
